protections: Security constraints declared with the Servlet 3.0 @ServletSecurity annotation on a servlet class are turned into SecurityConstraints and applied to that servlet's URL mappings, exactly like descriptor-declared constraints.

Security constraints added programmatically with ServletRegistration.setServletSecurity stay attached to every URL mapping of the servlet, and constraints already held for other URL patterns are preserved.

Every Context that has at least one security constraint gets an Authenticator valve (NonLoginAuthenticator when there is no login-config), so RealmBase's constraint checks are actually reached at request time.

Constraint matching for a request selects the constraints whose web-resource-collection matches the request path and the HTTP method, and a matching role-protected constraint denies access unless the authenticated principal holds a listed role.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The whole constraint-building machinery already exists and is exercised (StandardContext.addServletSecurity, ApplicationServletRegistration.setServletSecurity, SecurityConstraint.createConstraints, TestStandardContext.testBug50015), and ServletSecurityElement even has a constructor that takes the ServletSecurity annotation, so the annotation looks implemented; annotation processing also visibly runs in WebAnnotationSet and ContextConfig, inviting the conclusion that security annotations are covered.

The inline TODO says spec 13.4.2 is ambiguous about whether only the conflicting pattern or the whole security constraint is replaced, and today the branch is dead anyway because isFromDescriptor is always true (T4), so a solver can read it as an acknowledged spec ambiguity with no live effect.

The TODO at StandardContext.java:5643-5647 states outright that the spec requires the final constraint set to be computed when the context is started and that application code may add URL patterns after calling setSecurity, so a solver can treat the missing protection as a known, deliberate limitation.

The flag is internal bookkeeping, the conflict is returned to the caller as a set of URL patterns, and the application can see it, so a solver can conclude the behaviour is spec-conformant and that programmatic constraints never need to replace one another.

The Authenticator machinery exists and is installed for descriptor-declared constraints, and the project's own test for programmatic constraints adds a BasicAuthenticator valve by hand (test/org/apache/catalina/core/TestStandardContext.java:273), so a reader can assume an authenticator is the application's job or that the manual valve is the intended pattern.

The other three URL-matching branches all consult SecurityCollection.findMethod, so the last branch looks like a harmless special case for the root pattern, and a constraint that is added where it was not expected only looks more restrictive.

The carve-outs are needed for FORM login to work at all (login page, error page and the /j_security_check action must be reachable), and the form action always sits at the context root, so an endsWith test looks equivalent to an exact match.

masking: T2 only becomes reachable once T4 is fixed: because no code ever calls SecurityCollection.setFromDescriptor(false), isFromDescriptor is always true, so the overwrite branch at StandardContext.java:5625-5633 that removes the whole SecurityConstraint is dead today.

T3 and T4 only bite once constraints actually flow through StandardContext.addServletSecurity, which today happens only for ServletContainerInitializer/Listener programmatic registration (and would happen for annotations after T1 is fixed).

conflicts.what: The natural T1 fix routes annotation constraints through StandardContext.addServletSecurity, where the always-true isFromDescriptor conflict test (T4) silently drops an annotation constraint for any URL pattern that already has a constraint; fixing T1 without T4 leaves @ServletSecurity unenforced in exactly the mixed descriptor/annotation configurations the fix is meant to cover.

Setting isFromDescriptor(false) for programmatic and annotation constraints (the T4 fix) activates the overwrite branch that calls removeConstraint(securityConstraint) (StandardContext.java:5632), deleting the constraint for the other URL patterns of that constraint and losing a protection those patterns must keep.

fairness_risks: A servlet annotated with bare @ServletSecurity (default HttpConstraint is EmptyRoleSemantic.PERMIT with no roles) must stay openly accessible; SecurityConstraint.createConstraint deliberately returns null in that case (java/org/apache/catalina/deploy/SecurityConstraint.java:536-547), so a fix that treats any @ServletSecurity as protected would lock out legitimate servlets.

metadata-complete=true / Context.ignoreAnnotations must keep suppressing annotation-derived constraints (java/org/apache/catalina/startup/ContextConfig.java:876, java/org/apache/catalina/deploy/WebXml.java:1205); a fix that applies @ServletSecurity regardless breaks applications that opted out of annotation scanning.

Descriptor-declared constraints must keep precedence over @ServletSecurity for the same url-pattern: StandardContext.java:5621-5624 returns the pattern as a conflict instead of overwriting; a naive union would create duplicate or contradictory constraints for apps where web.xml is authoritative.

A security-constraint with url-pattern '/' and no http-method list must keep applying to all methods (SecurityCollection.findMethod returns true when both method arrays are empty, java/org/apache/catalina/deploy/SecurityCollection.java:246-249); the T6 fix must consult findMethod rather than drop default-pattern constraints.
A method-scoped constraint on '/' (for example GET only) is legitimate configuration: the refused shape is 'a / constraint that applies to a method it does not list', not '/ constraints' as a class.

Contexts that already supply an Authenticator valve must not get a second one when T5 is fixed (java/org/apache/catalina/startup/ContextConfig.java:380 short-circuits on getAuthenticator() != null), and contexts with no constraints must keep starting without an Authenticator.

design.why: These four sit at four different layers of the same protection and each has a distinct reason to dismiss, so they cannot be closed by one insight. T1 is a route where the protection never existed at all (the annotation driver is missing) while every surrounding piece exists and one constructor is already written for it - a deepseek-shaped absence. T5 is an ordering hole: the decision 'does this context need an Authenticator?' is taken at ContextConfig.java:885, before ServletContainerInitializer onStartup runs at StandardContext.java:5119, so programmatic constraints are created but never enforced, and the project's own test hides the hole by adding the valve by hand. T4 is a coupled default value (isFromDescriptor defaults to true and is never cleared), the mimo-shaped trap. T6 is a request-matching shape where one of four sibling branches omits the method check, which a solver will not see unless it compares the branches. Together they give two deepseek-flavoured and two mimo-flavoured independent judgements, with T2 as a latent fifth that T4's fix would unmask; a design built only on T1 would be a single-file treasure hunt, and a design built only on T3/T4/T2 would collapse into one rewrite of addServletSecurity.

unverified: The B fix commit 299b26af6679 is not in the pinned worktree and the clone's git objects lie outside the readable tree, so which trap it patches is inferred from code evidence: java/javax/servlet/ServletSecurityElement.java:87 is a fully implemented constructor that takes the ServletSecurity annotation and is never called by main code, next to a WebAnnotationSet that handles every other class-level servlet annotation.

The advisory text of GHSA-3xpj-jgv5-q4vv and of CVE-2011-1088 was not available in the worktree; identifying A with the Servlet 3.0 dynamic-security work is inferred from the in-tree test testBug50015 (test/org/apache/catalina/core/TestStandardContext.java:255) and from StandardContext.addServletSecurity being the only large access-control mechanism here.
Whether upstream ever closed T3, T4, T6 or T7 could not be checked; they are labelled uncovered_upstream on code evidence alone.
Whether T2 and T3 would be closed by the same redesign (deferring constraint computation to context start) is arguable, which is why they are listed as separate groups rather than merged.
Tier values are the supplied priors adjusted by judgement for this instance, not measured miss rates.
